exit_criteria.text: Downloads a 1 GB file correctly over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2
exit_criteria.evidence: tests/corpus/tests/gigabyte.rs, run by `just corpus-slow`. Verified 2026-08-03: 1 000 000 000 bytes over HTTP/1.1 (3.0s) and over HTTP/2 as h2c (3.6s), each compared byte for byte against blake3-ctr-v1 with 0 mismatches. The verifier itself is proven able to fail by a companion test that flips one byte 3 MiB in. Caveat recorded as backlog B-8: HTTP/2 here is cleartext h2c, not h2 over TLS with ALPN, which the corpus cannot yet express. ALSO VERIFIED IN CI, not only locally: the slow-corpus job in .github/workflows/ci.yml ran both gigabyte cases on a GitHub runner in 107 s (run 30829132772, triggered with `gh workflow run CI`). That matters because 'green on the machine that produced it' is the property CI exists to rule out.

exit_criteria.text: The capability probe correctly classifies range support on every 'ranges' corpus case
exit_criteria.evidence: 15 cases in tests/corpus/cases/ranges/, all passing, each asserting expect.range_support explicitly so the classification is checked rather than inferred from the download succeeding. They cover every range behaviour the pathology server can produce - correct 206, Accept-Ranges absent, Accept-Ranges lies, 206-with-whole-body, shifted Content-Range, omitted Content-Range, three malformed Content-Range shapes, unknown total length, multipart/byteranges for a single range, totals both overstated and understated - plus the proven path over h2c and with no validator and with a weak-ETag-only validator. Exactly one behaviour yields Proven; the other fourteen do not, and five of those answer with 206. I-6's proof list in docs/agent/INVARIANTS.md names three cases and all three now exist: accept-ranges-lies, head-differs-from-get (which also asserts NO HEAD request reached the server, since checking only the conclusion cannot distinguish 'ignored HEAD' from 'asked and got lucky'), and cdn-edge-disagrees (an edge that advertises ranges redirecting to an origin that does not honour them). Guarded mechanically from here on by tests/corpus/tests/invariant_proofs.rs, which parses INVARIANTS.md and fails if any named proof case neither exists nor is deferred with a stage and a reason. HONEST LIMIT: the category is 17 against docs/09 §3.2's initial target of 25; the remainder needs S2/S3 features and is tracked as B-13.

exit_criteria.text: Filename sanitisation passes its property tests including path-traversal cases

exit_criteria.text: Never writes a body received with an unexpected Content-Encoding
exit_criteria.evidence: Four layers, each asserted independently. Header level: crates/downpour-types/tests/range_proof.rs::a_gzipped_range_response_is_rejected. Probe level: tests/corpus/tests/probe.rs::a_compressed_ranged_response_is_an_error_not_a_downgrade, which also asserts it is NOT downgraded to RangeSupport::Absent - conflating those would let the transfer proceed over bytes that do not correspond to the representation. Request level: ::the_probe_sends_accept_encoding_identity, asserted against the request the SERVER recorded rather than against our own code. Filesystem level: tests/corpus/tests/download.rs::a_compressed_body_is_never_written asserts the target directory is EMPTY afterwards - not even a .dppart - and crates/downpour-cli/tests/dp_add.rs asserts exit 1 with no file. Mutation-checked: deleting the Content-Encoding check turns the first two red. Also structural: no decompression feature is enabled on reqwest, so there is no code path that could inflate a body.

exit_criteria.text: 'redirects' and 'framing' corpus categories pass
exit_criteria.evidence: Both categories are at or over docs/09 section 3.2's target and every case passes under `just gate`. framing 17/15: gzip-on-range, brotli, uppercase and padded non-identity tokens, a list containing identity, identity accepted in uppercase and padded form, chunked, close-delimited, chunked-short-but-well-formed, chunked-missing-terminator, truncated body, truncated after one byte, wrong Content-Length, HTML-instead-of-file, zero-length representation, and a body with no HTTP/1.1 length signal over h2c. redirects 10/10: mixed-status chain, 303, 308, loop bounded by the hop limit, chain over h2c, chain ending at an origin without range support, redirect with no Location, redirect to an unusable Location, cross-host handoff, and a cross-host chain that keeps its intra-origin hops. The last two assert expect.crosses_origin, without which they passed even with the cross-origin wiring disabled.

exit_criteria.text: Zero silent corruption across the S1 corpus subset
exit_criteria.evidence: 42 corpus cases, 0 silent-corruption findings, and the detector is proven able to fire rather than merely observed passing: ServerSpec::corrupt_from makes the server return the right length with inverted content from 32 KiB on, and tests/corpus/tests/runner_self_test.rs::the_runner_detects_a_server_that_serves_corrupt_bytes asserts the runner reports SILENT CORRUPTION naming byte 32768. Mutation-checked: disabling the comparison turns exactly that test red. The comparison is imposed by the runner on every case and is not a key a case can set (ADR-0010). Broadest single statement: 1 000 000 000 bytes byte-exact over HTTP/1.1 and h2c via `just corpus-slow`. metrics.silent_corruption_findings is 0, which the validator treats as a release blocker if it ever is not.

exit_criteria.text: A transient transport failure mid-body is retried and the download still completes byte-correctly; Retry-After is honoured exactly; back-off is per-origin
exit_criteria.evidence: Three corpus cases plus 15 unit tests. connections/transient-reset-is-retried: the first body request is truncated mid-transfer and the connection closed, and the download recovers to a byte-exact file - with expect.min_requests: 3 asserting a retry actually happened, without which the case would pass just as well if nothing had broken. connections/repeated-resets-exhaust-the-budget: every body fails, and the engine gives up after MAX_RETRIES instead of looping, leaving no final name (I-4). connections/retry-after-is-honoured: a 503 with Retry-After: 1 is waited out rather than replaced by our own back-off. crates/downpour-http/tests/retry_policy.rs pins the rest without a network: exact honouring of both delay-seconds and HTTP-date forms, malformed values falling back to computed back-off, absurd values clamped, the full status table including 408 as a timeout, and per-origin rather than per-worker accounting. All mutation-checked.

tasks.title: Pathology server: deterministic PRNG content, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, and the ranges/framing/redirects behaviours
tasks.proof: tests/corpus/tests/content_generator.rs (12 tests) and tests/corpus/tests/pathology_server.rs (29 tests), 41 total. Determinism: the server serves exactly the generator's bytes over both HTTP/1.1 and h2c, two servers with the same seed agree, and both protocols produce identical bytes. Pathologies verified against a reference client (hyper for h2, a hand-written reader for h1 - deliberately not downpour-http, which would be circular): accept-ranges-absent, accept-ranges-lies, 206-with-whole-body, shifted Content-Range, omitted Content-Range, literal malformed Content-Range, unknown total length, 416, chunked, close-delimited, wrong Content-Length, mid-body truncation, gzip-on-range, redirect chains, redirect loops, keep-alive reuse, request recording on both protocols, and an HTML error page where a binary was expected. Mutation-checked: making Lies honour ranges, ignoring truncate_body_after, and always emitting a correct Content-Range each turn red exactly the tests that claim those pathologies and no others.

tasks.title: The TransferProtocol trait and the h1h2 backend over reqwest/rustls
tasks.proof: crates/downpour-http/tests/trait_object.rs (9 tests). TransferProtocol is object-safe: usable as Box<dyn>, held in a Vec<Box<dyn>>, and shared across four tokio tasks as Arc<dyn> - which is what ADR-0005 rests on, since the simulator is just another backend. A stub backend satisfies the trait with no reqwest type in any signature, proving the abstraction does not leak. H1H2Backend coerces to the trait object and reports capabilities that differ by transport mode, so the scheduler never needs a version check. RangeSink is append-only from a fixed base offset, refuses a write past its grant whole rather than partially, and does not write anything on refusal (I-2 precondition); sync reaches the target (I-1 commit point). SCOPE LIMIT, stated rather than implied: h1h2::probe and h1h2::fetch_range are written but have NO behavioural test coverage yet - nothing has exercised them against a server. That is S1-T8's job and S1-T8's proof, and no exit criterion may be marked met on the strength of this task.

tasks.title: Capability probe: ranged GET, redirect-chain capture, validator and digest capture, HTML-instead-of-file detection
tasks.proof: tests/corpus/tests/probe.rs (19 tests) against PathologyServer. I-6: a validated 206 is the only behaviour that yields RangeSupport::Proven, and all seven others yield Absent - including the five that answer 206 (correct Content-Range with the whole body, shifted Content-Range, omitted Content-Range, malformed Content-Range, unknown total length). I-5: a gzipped ranged response returns ProbeError::ContentEncoding rather than downgrading to Absent, and Accept-Encoding: identity is asserted on the request the SERVER recorded, not on our own code. I-8: every redirect hop including the submitted URL is recorded, and a loop hits TooManyRedirects with a bounded request count. Also: HTML-instead-of-file, 401/403/410 -> needs_refresh distinguished from 500/503 -> unexpected_status, weak-ETag classification, digest capture, Content-Disposition traversal sanitised to a single component, and the probe over h2c. Mutation-checked: downgrading the gzip case, removing Accept-Encoding: identity, and taking total_length from Content-Length on a 206 each turn red exactly the test that claims it. PROOF FIELD REVISED from the original 'corpus categories ranges and redirects pass under just corpus'. That was a decomposition error on my part: it made this task's proof depend on S1-T10's runner and S1-T11's case files, which are separate deliverables. The behaviour is proven here; expressing it as declarative YAML inventory is S1-T11's job, and exit criterion S1-C2 still requires those cases, so the criterion holds that line rather than this task.

tasks.title: Single-stream download: .dppart target, Content-Encoding rejection, verify length and coverage and digest, then atomic rename
tasks.proof: tests/corpus/tests/download.rs (14 tests). I-4 asserted on every failure path: the final name is never created unless the delivered length matches what the probe established, and the assertions check the directory listing rather than only the return value. A truncated body leaves content.dppart holding bytes that still match the generator, so a later resume can trust them. I-5: a compressed body produces no file at all, not even a .dppart, because the probe rejects it first. Byte-exactness against the generator over HTTP/1.1, h2c, chunked framing, a redirect chain, and a server without range support. Plus: a Content-Disposition traversal lands inside the target directory, an existing file is never overwritten, and a zero-length representation still produces a file. FOUND AND FIXED TWO ENGINE DEFECTS while writing these, both caught by the new tests, both with their regression test in this change (Gate D): (1) the probe treated 416 as fatal, so an empty representation - or any server that refuses bytes=0-0 - could not be downloaded at all; docs/03 section 2.1 says a non-206 means single stream, not failure, so the probe now re-asks without a Range. (2) a body that died before its declared Content-Length surfaced as an opaque transport error, losing both that it was a truncation and how many bytes arrived, which docs/03 section 7 needs for its retry policy; now reported as TruncatedBody, detected from the length already known rather than by matching the HTTP library's error shape.

tasks.title: Corpus runner: YAML case to server configuration to engine run to assertions, wired to `just corpus`
tasks.proof: tests/corpus/tests/runner_self_test.rs (6 tests) - the fail-closed proof ADR-0010 requires - plus tests/corpus/tests/corpus_cases.rs (4 tests) which runs the whole case set. The two that matter: the_runner_fails_a_case_whose_expectation_is_wrong feeds the runner a fixture claiming a gzipped ranged response completes, and asserts the runner REJECTS it; and the_runner_detects_a_server_that_serves_corrupt_bytes has the server return the right length with correct headers and inverted content from 32 KiB on, and asserts a SILENT CORRUPTION finding naming byte 32768. That second one required adding ServerSpec::corrupt_from, and it is the most important self-test in the project: without a server that can serve wrong bytes, the runner's byte comparison is only ever observed passing, which is indistinguishable from a comparison that never runs. Mutation-checked: disabling the corruption check turns exactly that test red. Also asserted: an unknown key is a hard error naming the key (not a dropped assertion), a failure case with no error_kind is rejected, an unimplemented generator name is rejected rather than falling back, and a case describing mid-transfer `behaviour` is rejected because the server cannot enact it until S2. the_recorded_case_count_matches_reality pins metrics.corpus_cases_total to the files on disk so it cannot drift into a number nobody checks. YAML crate: serde_norway, recorded in docs/14.
tasks.notes: YAML crate research done 2026-08-03 so it need not be repeated. serde_yaml is DEPRECATED - its latest release is literally version 0.9.34+deprecated, last updated 2024-03-25 - so it must not be used. Live options, verified against crates.io: serde_norway 0.9.42 (a maintained fork of serde_yaml by cafkafk, updated 2024-12, 8.5M downloads, drop-in serde integration); serde_yaml_ng 0.10.0 (another fork, updated 2024-05, 7.6M downloads); yaml-rust2 0.11.0 (updated 2025-12, 49M downloads, but a low-level parser with no serde derive support, so the case structs would be hand-parsed); saphyr 0.0.11 (yaml-rust2's successor, actively developed, but still 0.0.x). RECOMMENDATION: serde_norway, because ADR-0010 requires the runner to FAIL CLOSED on an unknown key, which serde's deny_unknown_fields gives directly - and a hand-rolled parser would have to reimplement exactly that. Record it in docs/14 section 1 rather than writing an ADR: the cases are plain YAML data, so any conformant parser can read them and the choice is cheap to reverse. Remember the fail-closed requirement is the point of the task: also needed are the tests/corpus/self-test/ fixture whose deliberately-wrong expectation must make the runner FAIL, and the unconditional byte-comparison and file_renamed assertions that no case may opt out of.

tasks.title: 1 GB correctness over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2
tasks.proof: tests/corpus/tests/gigabyte.rs::a_gigabyte_over_http11_is_byte_exact and ::a_gigabyte_over_http2_is_byte_exact, run by `just corpus-slow` (release, --run-ignored all). Verified 2026-08-03: 1 000 000 000 bytes over HTTP/1.1 in 3.0s and over h2c in 3.6s, both compared byte for byte against the generator with 0 mismatches. Neither side holds a gigabyte: the server generates each chunk as it is polled and the verifier streams the file past the generator 1 MiB at a time. A third test, NOT ignored, corrupts one byte deep in the third window and asserts the verifier panics - without it the two gigabyte results would prove nothing. Ignored by default so the every-push budget stays under five minutes (docs/09 section 6). REQUIRED A SERVER FIX: the pathology server materialised the whole body in memory, which made a 1 GB case impossible and silently capped the corpus at what fits in RAM. Both protocols now stream from the generator, which is the reason the generator was made seekable in the first place.

tasks.title: Migrate CI to GitHub Actions and fix the pipeline that burned 400 GitLab minutes
tasks.proof: MEASURED, three runs on GitHub Actions. GitLab's last green pipeline: 1706 s = 28.4 min, Linux only, cache achieving nothing. GitHub cold with the new Windows job added: 412 s = 6.9 min. GitHub WARM: 196 s = 3.3 min for MORE coverage than GitLab ever had. Per job, cold -> warm: rust 112 s -> 38 s, windows 264 s -> 128 s, security 23-28 s (was 370-511 s on GitLab because it compiled cargo-audit every run), harness 5-8 s (was ~35 s across three jobs). Against GitLab that is 88 percent less compute while also testing Windows. Runs: 30826183828 (cold), 30826537689 (cold + windows), 30827248189 (warm). ADR-0011 records the diagnosis and the reversal triggers. Root causes fixed: tools now arrive as prebuilt binaries (taiki-e/install-action on GitHub, cargo-binstall on GitLab) instead of being compiled; one Rust job replaces four so the workspace compiles once; the redundant corpus job is gone because nextest --workspace already covered it; and the cache includes ~/.cargo/bin, which is the entry whose absence made every `cargo install` recompile from scratch. GitLab's config is kept current and disabled at .gitlab-ci.yml.disabled so re-enabling is a rename.

tasks.title: Retry and back-off: the 'robust' half of the stage title is not implemented
tasks.proof: crates/downpour-http/tests/retry_policy.rs (15 unit tests on the pure policy) plus three corpus cases that prove recovery end to end: connections/transient-reset-is-retried, connections/repeated-resets-exhaust-the-budget, connections/retry-after-is-honoured. The success case would have been VACUOUS on its own - it expects , which also happens when the injected failure does nothing - so expect.min_requests was added to the case format and the runner now asserts the server saw at least 3 requests (probe + failed body + retried body). Mutation-checked three ways: disabling the retry loop makes both retry cases fail WITH the min_requests message naming that no retry occurred; making the server never inject the failure makes the exhaustion case fail AND trips min_requests on the success case; and neutralising the magic-byte sniff makes the lying-content-type case fail. The corpus runner uses RetryPolicy::fast_for_tests because truncation cases now legitimately retry five times first, which at the spec's real delays cost 72 s for the case set - it is 6.6 s now, and the real values stay pinned by the unit tests. max_server_delay is deliberately NOT shortened, so retry-after-is-honoured still waits the full second the server asked for.

exit_criteria.text: Crash injection at every write boundary yields a byte-correct file after resume
exit_criteria.evidence: tests/sim/tests/crash_matrix.rs injects a failure at each of the six boundaries in write, data sync, journal append, journal sync and Complete, then rebuilds state from the durable artifacts alone. crash_at_every_write_boundary_recovers_byte_exact asserts a pre-crash block always survives, that a range past the journal sync is never lost, that nothing is claimed when nothing was written, that every claimed byte matches downpour_corpus::content::Content — an oracle that knows nothing about how we wrote them — and that the in-memory interval map never claims a range the journal cannot support. resuming_after_a_crash_at_any_boundary_produces_the_whole_file then resumes from the recovered prefix and compares the finished file byte for byte. The reordering that moves the map before the journal sync makes the first of these go red, which is the specific corruption this criterion exists to catch. just gate 283 tests (3 skipped) and just sim 8/8 across 3 fixed seeds, re-run 2026-08-05 after the symlink work. The crash matrix also runs on Windows: tests/sim is a workspace member, so CI's windows job executes it under `cargo nextest run --workspace`, which is what makes G2's 'on Linux and Windows' a checked claim rather than an assumed one. HARDENED 2026-08-05 (S2-T16), and the criterion did not previously hold in the way this field implied. The proof of I-1's ORDERING is DurableWriter's own sequence test, completion_is_never_observable_before_data_and_journal_are_durable; the crash matrix proves RECOVERY is byte-exact given that ordering. Until this change the matrix could not tell the two apart, because CrashingData wrote straight through and so never lost an unsynced byte: inverting the two syncs in flush passed all 8 simulations. CrashingData now buffers like CrashingJournal, and Boundary::DataSyncIssued adds the crash point in the window between the syncs. The inversion now fails with "DataSyncIssued: claimed range [8192, 16384) does not match the generator".

exit_criteria.text: Zero silent corruption across the whole corpus so far
exit_criteria.evidence: 76 of 76 corpus cases pass with zero corruption findings, verified on 2026-08-05 by just corpus (94 tests, 3 skipped) and the full slow set (97, 0 skipped). The criterion is worded 'across the whole corpus SO FAR', which scopes it to the cases that exist, and every one of them passes the runner's unconditional byte comparison against downpour_corpus::content::Content — an oracle that knows nothing about how the bytes were written. That comparison is itself mutation-verified from both directions: tests/corpus/tests/runner_self_test.rs::the_runner_detects_a_server_that_serves_corrupt_bytes for a finished file and ::the_runner_detects_corrupt_bytes_in_an_unfinished_part_file for a preallocated .dppart, so a comparison that silently stopped running would be caught rather than reported as green. NOTE the limit of this claim, restated honestly now that local is closed: docs/09's inventory stands at 76 of 159 overall. The categories S2 owns are complete or past target — validators 16/15, framing 16/15, redirects 10/10, local 12/12 — and ranges is at 17 of 25. What is thin is what later stages own: session 2/20, connections 3/20, and proxies, protocols and media at zero because the features they describe do not exist yet. So the claim is strong about the pathologies S2 can reach and says nothing about the ones it cannot; B-13 carries ranges and the empty categories belong to their own stages.

tasks.notes: A gate review that only re-ran the suites would have passed S2. This task exists because the suites were asked the harder question — can each exit proof fail in the direction it claims? — and two could not. THE ENGINE WAS CORRECT IN BOTH CASES. What was wrong was the evidence, which is the more dangerous defect: a green proof that cannot go red is indistinguishable from a proof, right up until a refactor removes the behaviour and nothing says so. (1) S2-C1/I-1. Inverting the durability ordering in DurableWriter::flush — syncing the journal before the data, the exact reordering docs/agent/INVARIANTS.md and .claude/rules/engine.md call non-negotiable — passed all 8 simulations. The cause was an asymmetry in the harness: CrashingJournal buffers unsynced appends and loses them on a crash, and its doc comment explains precisely why that is what makes the simulation faithful, but CrashingData wrote straight through to the real part file. So the part file always held every byte ever passed to write_all_at, whether or not a sync followed, and the byte comparison could never fail. Fixed by buffering data writes the same way, and by adding Boundary::DataSyncIssued — the crash point in the window between the two syncs, symmetric with the existing JournalSync. Only that pair can observe an ordering, as opposed to bookkeeping. The inversion now fails with a byte mismatch on the claimed range. (2) S2-C3/I-2. Deleting the Pending guard from IntervalMap::grant — the check that stops the same byte range being handed to two workers — passed all 283 tests, and RangeNotPending had no test anywhere in the repository. The property test asserted only that a REJECTED grant left the map unchanged, never that an ACCEPTED one should have been, and replace_range keeps the partition canonical whatever it is handed: a double grant silently transfers the bytes and disjoint-and-total still holds. So the tested property was strictly weaker than I-2, which is about exclusive ownership rather than structure. Fixed by asserting the only-if contract for both grant and complete, computed from the map before the call. Not yet live — there is one writer until S3's allocator — which is exactly why it was worth closing now, before the stage that makes it live. Checked and found genuinely well-guarded, so no change: S2-C2 (disabling both journal CRC checks reddens 3 tests including the named one), S2-C5 (a one-byte over-claim in durable_bytes_after_disk_full reddens both disk-full tests; an earlier staged-bytes mutation passed only because that state is unreachable, a no-op mutation rather than a gap), S2-C6 (neutering check_coverage reddens no_incomplete_map_is_ever_renamed), and IntervalMap::complete's ownership guard, which two durable_writer tests already caught.

S2. The pass rate G7 measures is 100 percent — 76 of 76, zero corruption findings — but the matrix it is measured over is roughly half built, and the scoring rules say to score the fraction that actually works rather than the fraction of what exists. backlog.text: CLOSED 2026-08-10 by S3-T10. Its earlier wording said recovery trusting the journal "is the documented `off` mode, which is the correct default". That is wrong and is repaired here rather than left to be read again: docs/04 section 3.4 is normative and names `sample` as the default, with `off` as the fastest opt-out. Treating `off` as the default would have made the shipped behaviour quietly weaker than the spec while looking compliant. verify_on_resume now exists as off, sample and full. Sample selection is derived from the transfer id and the block sequence rather than an RNG, so the same journal always samples the same blocks — reproducible for a user reporting a fault, and full is then a superset of what sample checked. A block whose part bytes no longer hash to its recorded BLAKE3 is excluded before the interval map is built, so its range returns to Pending and is fetched again; nothing is rehashed into the journal and the journal is not rewritten, because recomputing a digest from bytes that just failed would bless the corruption into durable evidence. Original: docs/04 section 3.4's verify_on_resume config (off / sample 1% / full) is not implemented.
backlog.rationale: The backlog said off was the correct default and the normative spec says sample; a backlog that contradicts the spec is how the weaker behaviour ships looking finished

backlog.text: FIXED 2026-08-05: the Stop-hook RECORD guard fired on changes whose progress record had already been written and committed alongside them. .claude/hooks/progress-guard.sh read the record's mtime with `stat -c %Y`, which truncates to whole seconds, then compared with `find -newermt "@<seconds>"`, which compares at nanosecond precision against <seconds>.000000000. Every file carrying a sub-second mtime therefore read as newer, including state/progress.json itself, and `git checkout` and `git merge` stamp every file they write with one shared sub-second mtime. Fixed to `find -newer "$PROGRESS"`, a direct file-to-file comparison at full precision. scripts/test-progress-guard.sh now asserts both directions and is wired into `just gate`.
backlog.rationale: It fired three times in one session on work that was correctly recorded. The dangerous outcome is not the noise itself but the habit it teaches: an agent that learns the RECORD guard is noise will dismiss it on the day it is right, which is the exact drift the guard exists to prevent

backlog.text: RESOLVED 2026-08-05. Not flakiness — a real user-facing bug introduced in S2-T8. Reproduced by saturating all 16 cores and running the workspace at 48 test threads: downpour-cli::dp_add::dp_add_downloads_from_a_server_without_range_support failed 2 of 6 runs. Cause: `dp` resolves its journal directory to the shared XDG data dir, names each journal blake3(final_url)[..16].dpj, creates it exclusively, and B-22 meant a successful download never deleted it. Ephemeral ports are recycled, so a reused port reproduces the same final URL, hits the previous run's journal, and the exclusive create fails the whole download. 185 leaked journals were found in the developer's real home directory. The user-visible form is worse than the test symptom: download a file, delete it, download it again, and it fails. Fixed by docs/04 section 6 step 10 — delete the journal after verification passes and the rename succeeds — which S2-T11 made safe. Regression test: tests/corpus/tests/download.rs::the_same_url_can_be_downloaded_twice. Verified with 8 runs under the same saturation, zero failures.
backlog.rationale: An intermittently red suite is worse than a red one: it trains everyone to re-run until green, which is exactly how a real defect gets classified as noise. Recorded with its exact observation so the next session starts from evidence rather than from memory

backlog.text: PROMOTED AND FIXED 2026-08-05. Filed as an S3 tidiness item about unbounded journal growth; it was actually the same user-facing fault as B-29 reached from the other side. A FAILED download keeps its journal deliberately, because it is evidence a resume depends on — but that journal then collided with the next attempt's exclusive create, so one failure poisoned its URL forever and the download the user most wants to retry is exactly the one they could not. It resurfaced as the same intermittent dp_add failure B-29 produced, because leaked journals accumulate and recycled ephemeral ports reproduce a final URL. Fixed in StorageSink::create: the part file is created exclusively first, so getting past it proves no other owner holds this target, which makes any journal still at that path orphaned — it has no part file to protect and nothing can be resumed from it — and safe to replace. Regression test tests/corpus/tests/download.rs::a_failed_download_does_not_block_a_later_attempt_at_the_same_url, which uses ONE server so both attempts resolve to the same URL; a first version used two and passed without exercising anything. Verified with four full-workspace runs under 16-core saturation at 48 test threads. The retention policy of docs/04 section 8 remains unimplemented and is now the only part of this entry left, targeted at S3.
backlog.rationale: Found while verifying the B-29 fix. Unbounded growth in a user's home directory is a real defect even though each individual retention is correct

backlog.text: ANALYSED 2026-08-05. local stands at 10 of docs/09's 12, and the remaining two classes appear NOT to be corpus-expressible, which is a defect in the inventory rather than work outstanding. (1) Disk full mid-transfer, end to end through the engine: the corpus runs the real SingleStream against a real filesystem, so bounding the volume would need either a controllable filesystem — not portable, and root-only where it is possible — or a fault-injection hook inside StorageSink, which would put test scaffolding in the production write path. tests/sim covers the same property at the storage layer with a bounded volume, which is where injection belongs. (2) Network filesystems: an NFS or SMB mount cannot be created in-process, and the pathologies that matter — silent write reordering, a server that acknowledges an fsync it did not perform — are precisely the ones a local mount would not reproduce. PROPOSAL for the maintainer: rewrite docs/09's local target from 12 to 10 and record that disk-full is owned by tests/sim and network filesystems by manual qualification, OR keep 12 and accept the category can never honestly close. Not changing the spec unilaterally.
backlog.rationale: Recorded rather than padded: docs/09 asks for distinct pathologies and the honest blocker is missing vocabulary, not missing YAML

backlog.text: Two assertions in the corpus cannot be falsified by mutating current code, and are recorded rather than counted as proven. The pre-existing-target survival check in the runner is belt-and-braces: the engine refuses before creating anything, so the file survives whether or not the check runs, and the case would already fail on its error_kind. And the read-only-directory refusal branch — which declines to report a pass when the process bypasses permission checks — is unreachable for an unprivileged user, so it is never exercised on a normal developer machine or in CI. Both guard future regressions. If CI ever runs as root the second becomes live, and that is the point at which it should be verified rather than assumed.
backlog.rationale: An assertion that no mutation can break is not proven, only present; saying so is cheaper than rediscovering it when one of them silently stops working

backlog.text:
ADR-0017's reversal trigger has FIRED, and the measurement it required exists. A 1 GB download completes in 6.2s with no server digest and 12.0s with one — 162 MB/s against 83 MB/s — because verification streams the whole file a second time after the transfer. That is not a margin, it is half the total time, which is the 'verification dominating completion for large files' the ADR named. The fix the ADR also named is to compute the SHA-2 incrementally as bytes arrive rather than to stop verifying: the writer already hashes every block with BLAKE3 on the way past, so a second hasher over the same bytes costs one pass instead of two. It is deliberately NOT done here — docs/agent/HARNESS.md says not to optimise before the stage's correctness gate is green, and an optimisation in the verification path needs a test showing behaviour is unchanged, which is its own piece of work. Numbers reproduce with `cargo nextest run -p downpour-corpus --release --run-ignored all -E 'test(/gigabyte/)'`.

REFINED 2026-08-05, and the refinement matters more than the measurement. ADR-0017 suggests fixing this by computing the SHA-2 incrementally as bytes arrive. That is UNSOUND past S2. SHA-2 is order-dependent, and DurableWriter::stage takes an arbitrary offset because S3's segment allocator hands different ranges to different workers — bytes stop arriving in offset order the moment segmentation lands, so a hasher fed in arrival order would produce a digest for a byte sequence that is not the file. It would work in S2, pass every test written today, and start silently failing every digest comparison in S3 for a reason nobody would look for. BLAKE3 has a combiner for exactly this shape, which is why the journal uses it per block; SHA-2 does not, and the server chooses the algorithm. So the real options are: accept the second pass as inherent whenever bytes can arrive out of order, overlap it with the transfer rather than following it, or hash incrementally only while the transfer is provably a single sequential stream and fall back otherwise — which is a conditional in the verification path and needs to earn its complexity. ADR-0017 should be superseded rather than stretched if the third is chosen.
backlog.rationale: ADR-0017 accepted this cost explicitly and made the measurement the precondition for revisiting it; taking the measurement without recording that the trigger fired would leave the accepted cost looking unexamined

backlog.text: FIXED 2026-08-10 by the B-37 half of S3-T9, ahead of the resume half it was targeted at. FOUND 2026-08-05 while fixing the try_exists symlink bug in SingleStream::download. The same follows-links hazard exists at crates/downpour-storage/src/recovery.rs:238, which tests reachability with metadata.part_path.exists(). If part_path were a symlink to a real file, exists() reports true and recovery goes on to PartFile::open_existing, which opens through the link and would write the resumed download over the destination. NOT EXPLOITABLE TODAY, and that is why it is recorded rather than fixed in this change: the part file is created with create_new, which refuses a symlink, so one can only appear if something replaces it between a crash and a recovery; and the path that would write through it does not run, because resume is still in-call only (B-25) and S2-T14 leaves recovered downloads paused. It becomes live the moment cross-process resume lands, which is why this is targeted there and not later. Fixing it properly means deciding a policy rather than swapping a call: symlink_metadata answers the reachability question without following, but the open that follows it needs O_NOFOLLOW to close the window completely, and that is a platform-specific flag with a Windows counterpart to choose. It needs a storage-layer test, not a corpus case: the corpus cannot reach recovery at all while resume is in-call only.
backlog.rationale: The corpus caught this class once already, at the download path, where it was live and silent. Recording the second instance with its exact reachability argument is what stops it being rediscovered by a user instead of by us

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10 by gate review, measured not inferred. FixedWorkerPool::execute_segmented collapses to one in-flight request after the first segment finishes. crates/downpour-engine/src/worker_pool.rs:364 cancels EVERY other running worker whenever any worker completes; the drain empties the JoinSet; :313 then allocates one split and spawns exactly one worker before `continue`, so the loop waits on that single worker. The parked peers keep their InProgress intervals and are not restarted until segments are too small to split and the :335 active_grants path fires. Measured with a temporary sim scenario (8 workers, 4096 bytes, near-equal 10 vs 11 ms/byte connection budgets, uncapped origin, in-flight counted through a Drop guard so cancelled requests stop counting): in-flight goes 8 at t=0, 7 at the first completion, 0 when the peers are cancelled, then fifteen consecutive rounds of exactly one in-flight request, then 7 again only at the unsplittable tail. Eight segments cost 32 requests. NOT A CORRECTNESS BUG: the final file was byte-exact and reported bytes summed to exactly 4096 in every run, because the drain is what makes I-2 trivially true. The drain is also unnecessary for safety — the state actor already rejects a stale write against the current map (writer_service.rs:391) and split_in_progress shortens the source atomically — so only the split's source needs stopping, and any worker whose grant is live but has no task needs respawning. This is docs/12's S3 deliverable 'split the largest remaining segment' behaving as one connection for most of a transfer.
backlog.rationale: S3 exists to make N connections faster than one. A design that serialises after the first completion delivers the opposite while passing a proof that cannot see it

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10 by gate review. The connection-reuse proof asserts a library's internal scheduling rather than engine behaviour. crates/downpour-http/src/h1h2.rs:58 builds the reqwest client with no pool configuration at all, and no engine code binds a worker to a connection; the comment at worker_pool.rs:319 describes a hoped-for checkout order, not a mechanism. worker_pool.rs:692 then asserts an exact connection_id match, which is why the same source is green on Linux (20/20 in isolation) and intermittently red on Windows. Compounding it, B-38's drain cancels in-flight responses on every completion, and a cancelled HTTP/1.1 response destroys its connection — so the current design re-handshakes peers on each completion event, which is the opposite of the criterion. Replace the assertion with accepted-handshake count, which the engine can influence, and fix B-38 first so the count means something.
backlog.rationale: A proof that flips colour between OSes on identical source teaches the team to re-run CI rather than to read it, which is how a real Windows failure gets waved through later

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10 by gate review. S3's headline deliverable is not reachable from the product and no task anywhere plans to wire it. crates/downpour-daemon/src/server.rs:123 runs SingleStream for every download and :79 refuses connections > 1 with segmented_execution_not_ready; :236 refuses download.resume with resume_not_ready. FixedWorkerPool and WriterService appear in zero non-test files outside crates/downpour-engine/src. The refusal itself is correct and is deliberately proven by S3-T8's an_unwired_multi_connection_request_is_refused_instead_of_silently_running_single — honest failure beats a silent single stream. The gap is planning, not honesty: S3-T9 through S3-T15 do not include the wiring, and S4 currently has no tasks, so as scheduled S3 closes with dynamic segmentation unavailable to any user. Decide explicitly whether the wiring is an S3 task or an S4 one and record it; do not let it fall between the two.
backlog.rationale: An exit criterion about connection count that no user can exercise is a criterion about a library, and the roadmap does not say so

backlog.text: FIXED 2026-08-10 in the same change as B-38. crates/downpour-engine did not declare tokio's `macros` feature although worker_pool.rs has always used tokio::select!. `cargo build -p downpour-engine` failed on develop with E0433 `cannot find select in tokio`; it only ever compiled because another workspace member enables `macros` and cargo unifies features. CI runs --workspace exclusively, so nothing caught it. Worth knowing that the same hole exists for any other under-declared feature in this workspace, and that a per-crate build is the only thing that finds it.
backlog.rationale: A crate that compiles only because of its neighbours is a crate that breaks the day it is built alone, published, or moved

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10 while mutation-auditing the B-38 fix, and deliberately left open. Scheduler::record_stopped_attempt flushes before it snapshots, so a stopped attempt's bytes are measured after its ownership is fenced. Removing that flush passes every test in the workspace. It is a no-op in every scenario reachable today, not a gap in the guard: WriterService::allocate flushes before any ownership change (ADR-0019 step 3), and the pool only sends a cancellation after an allocate has already run, so a stopped worker's staged bytes are committed before the measurement. The ordering that would need it is narrow and currently unreachable: the source stages one more write after that allocate's flush and before its task observes the cancellation. Its bytes would then be staged rather than Complete at the snapshot, would be omitted from that attempt's report, and would be committed by the *next* allocate's flush with no report to attribute them to, so the per-attempt sum would fall short of the representation length while the file itself stayed byte-exact. Reaching it deterministically needs an origin that can stage a write at a point it cannot currently observe. Recorded rather than removed, because deleting a load-bearing line that no test can defend is how the ordering gets reintroduced later by someone reading it as dead weight.
backlog.rationale: The S2 review's lesson was that a mutation surviving is a question, not an answer; this one was chased to a reachability argument rather than filed as either a hole or a pass

backlog.text: FIXED 2026-08-10 by S3-T16, and only found because the pool was wired to a real transfer. GrantWriter::write refused any payload above MAX_WRITE_BLOCK_BYTES (256 KiB) with BlockTooLarge, which the sink turned into a fatal TransferError::Sink. Every test until now used fixtures small enough that no single body chunk reached the bound; an 8 MiB download over loopback delivered a 363414-byte chunk and the whole transfer failed at offset 4813824. The handle now splits an oversized payload across several bounded commands, so the queue stays bounded in bytes — which is what the limit is actually for — and the BlockTooLarge variant is gone rather than left as an unreachable error with a test that could no longer fail. The general lesson is worth keeping: a bound expressed in bytes must be enforced by chunking somewhere, and 'the caller will not exceed it' is not enforcement when the caller is the network.
backlog.rationale: A limit that turns a normal-sized network chunk into a failed download is a bug that only appears at realistic sizes, which is exactly the class small fixtures cannot find

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10 while fixing B-37, and fixed in the same change. crates/downpour-storage/src/recovery.rs tested part-file presence with Path::exists(), which follows links, so it could not tell a dangling symlink from an absent file or a directory from a part file. A dangling symlink read as absent and failed the download as storage.part-file-missing, which is the answer that lets a later exclusive create follow the link and write through it — the same family as B-30 and B-37 reached from a third side. A directory read as present, so reconciliation went on to open it and reported whatever errno that produced, indistinguishable from a transient fault. Both are now storage.part-file-not-regular. The no-follow open alone did not cover either: reverting the presence check left both symlink proofs green, which is why the dangling-link and directory shapes have their own case.
backlog.rationale: The no-follow open makes the write safe; the presence check is what makes the diagnosis true, and a wrong diagnosis is what routes the next attempt into the same hazard

backlog.text: FOUND and FIXED 2026-08-10 while starting the resume half of S3-T9. The segmented worker pool issued every ranged request unconditionally: run_ranged_worker used RangeRequest::ranged, never RangeRequest::resume, so no worker request carried If-Range even though the constructor for it already existed. Harmless while a segmented transfer could only ever be one fresh session, and a live I-3 violation the moment cross-process resume writes into the holes of a file whose other bytes came from an earlier representation. Demonstrated rather than argued: with If-Range removed, a four-connection transfer against a server that swaps its ETag after an eighth of the body SUCCEEDS, exits zero and names the file — two representations spliced at exactly the expected size, which the length check and the coverage check both pass. Now sent on fresh transfers too, not only resumes: the cost is one header, and it turns a representation swapped between the probe and a worker request into a 200 the pool already refuses.
backlog.rationale: I-3 is one of the three invariants the roadmap says every open-source download manager has shipped broken; finding it unenforced on the path that is about to make it reachable is exactly what the resume task was supposed to surface

backlog.text: CAUGHT 2026-08-10 during the B-25 groundwork, in a test I had just written. The first version of the journal symlink proof planted a victim containing 37 bytes of plain text. Removing O_NOFOLLOW left it green, because the reopen failed on the header read — the victim was too short to hold a 72-byte header — rather than on the link. The property under test was never exercised. Rewritten so the victim is itself a valid journal carrying the same header, so a reopen that follows the link succeeds and the appended record lands in the victim; that version goes red under the mutation with the assertion naming what it cost. The general shape is worth keeping: a negative test whose fixture cannot reach the guard passes for a reason unrelated to the guard, and the only way to tell is to mutate the guard and watch. Both B-37 storage proofs were checked the same way afterwards and do fail correctly.
backlog.rationale: A refusal test is only evidence if the thing it refuses would otherwise have succeeded, and a fixture too small to reach the check silently guarantees it would not

backlog.text: FIXED 2026-08-10, and it was mine. A temporary eprintln debug probe — PROBE segmented failure — was added to crates/downpour-engine/src/segmented.rs while diagnosing B-43 and got committed in the S3-T16 change. Nothing caught it: clippy allows print_stdout and print_stderr by default, the engine crate deny list covered unwrap, expect, panic, todo, unimplemented and unreachable but not printing, and the file compiled and passed 333 tests with it in place. A debug print in a library is noise on a user terminal that no log level can turn off, and in the daemon it goes nowhere useful at all. The seven library crates now deny print_stdout and print_stderr in the same cfg_attr(not(test)) block that already denies the panic family, which is the existing house pattern; binaries and tests are untouched, because printing is their interface. Verified by reinstating the exact probe and watching clippy refuse it. The general point is the one the harness makes about corpus cases: the fix is not deleting the line, it is the guard that stops the next one.
backlog.rationale: A review standard applied to other agents work and not to my own is not a standard; the lint is what makes it one

backlog.text: FIXED 2026-08-10 while opening the daemon half of B-25. TransferDaemon minted download ids from 128 random bits, but those same sixteen bytes are the SQLite primary key and the recovery journal transfer id, and downpour_storage::metadata::DownloadId::try_from_bytes validates them as a UUIDv7. A random id satisfies the version and variant bits by accident roughly once in sixty-four, so persisting would have failed for about 98 percent of downloads with a validation error about UUID bits that has nothing to do with the download — and passed for the rest, which is the worst shape a bug can have. Nothing caught it because the daemon persists nothing yet: the id crossed no boundary where it was checked. Now a real UUIDv7, hand-rolled rather than adding a crate for twenty lines, with the leading 48 bits a millisecond timestamp so ids sort by creation and the primary-key index appends rather than inserting into the middle. Proven over 256 ids, because a single sample passes by chance often enough to be a flaky green.
backlog.rationale: An identifier that is valid at one layer and rejected at the next is not a small bug when the two layers are the IPC surface and the durable record that makes resume possible

backlog.text: PROCESS, recorded 2026-08-10 because it cost a red CI and has now happened three times in one session. Mutation-verifying with `git checkout -- <file>` to restore silently discards uncommitted work in that file, because it restores from HEAD rather than from before the mutation. It destroyed the If-Range implementation once, the writer-service Complete command once, and the UUIDv7 minter once — the third time the revert happened after the local gate and before the commit, so a test landed without the implementation it tested and GitHub caught it with a private-function error rather than a failing assertion. The mitigation is mechanical, not attentional: copy the file to a scratch path before mutating and restore from that copy, or commit before mutating. Saying commit first and then not doing it is what happened twice already.
backlog.rationale: A verification technique that can quietly delete the thing being verified will eventually produce a green mutation run against code that is not there

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10 while mapping stored lifecycle states onto the wire. downpour_storage DownloadState has AwaitingRefresh and downpour_ipc WireState does not, so the daemon cannot report a download that is waiting for a fresh URL. Nothing in S3 produces that state — URL refresh is S8 — so it is mapped to Paused with a comment rather than silently to Stalled, which would be wrong in a way a client acts on: Stalled promises automatic progress under backoff and AwaitingRefresh is waiting for a human or the extension. The wire needs the variant before S8 makes the state reachable, and adding one is an IPC contract change that belongs with the protocol version bump rather than here.
backlog.rationale: A state the daemon can be in and cannot report is a client that shows the wrong thing; collapsing it into a neighbouring state quietly is worse than the gap

backlog.text: FIXED 2026-08-10, and it would have made cross-process resume impossible. The engine named recovery journals from a blake3 of the final URL, with a comment saying it did so because no id allocator existed until the daemon owned one; the daemon startup pass looks for <journal_dir>/<download-id>.dpj exactly as docs/04 section 1 lays it out. So the engine wrote journals the daemon own recovery could never find, and every recovered download would have failed as journal-unreadable. StorageLayout::with_transfer_id now lets the allocated id name the journal, the daemon passes its own download id, and the URL hash stays the fallback for callers that have no allocator. Caught by the first end-to-end restart test rather than by reading, which is the argument for writing that test before the plumbing rather than after. Note on the proof: the first version of the restart test did NOT cover this — a completed download is terminal, reconciliation skips it, so the journal name never mattered and reverting the fix left the test green. The assertion that catches it checks, while the transfer is still live, that the journal exists at the path startup recovery will look for; reverting the fix now fails with "startup recovery looks for <id>.dpj, but the engine wrote <url-hash>.dpj". Worth remembering that the end-to-end test passing was not evidence for the thing it was written alongside.
backlog.rationale: Two components deriving the same filename by different rules is not a naming preference; it is a resume that silently never finds anything

backlog.text: FIXED 2026-08-10 in the same change. The daemon wrote a download record after the probe and never updated it, so a finished transfer stayed Transferring in the store forever. The next process then reconciled it against a part file that had been renamed away and failed it as storage.part-file-missing — a completed download reported as broken. Records now reach Completed or Failed when the transfer ends. Separately, recover() seeded the registry only from downloads reconciliation touched, and reconciliation deliberately skips terminal ones, so a completed download vanished from download.get after a restart; the registry is now seeded from the store, which is what it is a cache of.
backlog.rationale: A durable record that only ever describes the beginning of a transfer is worse than none, because recovery believes it

backlog.text: FIXED 2026-08-10 as the first part of S3-T11, and it was the blocker for the whole category. tests/corpus/src/runner.rs drove SingleStream and nothing else, so every corpus case ran on one connection. A per-IP cap, a per-connection cap and a concurrent-request limit only exist when more than one connection is open, which made the entire connections category unreachable rather than merely unwritten — and a case written for it would have passed while proving nothing. Cases now carry a  field and route to SegmentedDownload when it is above one. Found by writing the capped case and watching the new min_refused_connections assertion report that the cap never bit; without that assertion the case would have been green and vacuous. Note for the remaining cases: the segmented path uses RetryPolicy::default rather than fast_for_tests, so a concurrency case that also injects transient failures will be slow until the pool takes a policy.
backlog.rationale: A category the harness cannot reach is worse than an empty one, because cases written for it look like coverage

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10, not fixed. docs/03 section 9 lists STALL_WINDOW at 30 seconds with the note "No progress -> Stalled", and section 9 opens by saying every default there is configurable. It is implemented nowhere: grep finds Stalled only as an enum variant in the IPC, metadata and retry vocabularies, with nothing that measures progress against a window or moves a download into that state. What exists instead is a hardcoded 300-second per-request timeout in RangeRequest::whole, ranged and resume, which has no parameter behind it in the spec and is not reachable from configuration or from a corpus case. The practical consequence is that a server which accepts a connection and then never answers, or trickles bytes forever, is untestable: the only observable is a five-minute timeout, which no corpus case can wait for, and the correct answer per the spec is a 30-second stall window rather than a request deadline. Two connections-category pathologies named in docs/09 section 3.2 are blocked behind this. Deliberately not implemented here: a Stalled state machine is engine behaviour with its own proofs and is not among S3 deliverables in docs/12.
backlog.rationale: A normative parameter with no implementation is worse than a missing feature, because the spec reads as though the behaviour exists and nothing contradicts it

backlog.text: FIXED 2026-08-10 and it was a regression against S2. crates/downpour-engine/src/worker_pool.rs retryable_worker_failure mapped every TransferError::UnexpectedStatus to None, so one 429 or 503 on one worker failed the whole segmented download. The single-stream path has never done this: download.rs transient_kind_of runs the status through TransientKind::from_status and retry_after_of hands the header to the policy. So the S3 path was strictly less resilient than the S2 path it takes over from, against the signal I-7 names first. The pool now uses the same classification and passes Retry-After through; 401, 403 and 410 still return None because those belong to the refresh flow (I-8). Found by writing a-polite-cap-answers-429-instead-of-dropping, which failed with 'answered 429 where a body was expected' — no amount of reading the retry code would have shown it, because the retry code is correct and it was the classification in front of it that was not.
backlog.rationale: A cap enforced politely is more common than one enforced by dropping, and the polite one was the fatal case

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10, not fixed. A truncated body on the segmented path reports error_kind segmented_transfer; the single-stream path reports truncated_body for the identical server behaviour. Clients switch on kind and never on message (docs/08 section 3), so a client cannot tell 'the server cut the body' from 'the scheduler broke' — and only one of those is worth retrying or reporting to a user. DownloadError::Segmented should report its source's kind when the source is a transfer error. Deliberately not changed here: a kind is API, so it wants the protocol version bump rather than a corpus commit. tests/corpus/cases/connections/a-transfer-that-always-dies-at-the-same-offset-is-not-renamed asserts the current kind with a comment saying it is asserted as it is, not as it should be, so this cannot be fixed without the case being updated.
backlog.rationale: Two paths reporting different kinds for one server behaviour makes the kind useless to the client it exists for

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10. Two connections-category shapes remain blocked behind B-54's missing stall window, as recorded when that item was opened: a silent connection drop with no FIN, which needs idle-timeout detection per worker, and an origin that accepts a connection and then trickles or never answers. Both are observable only as the hardcoded 300-second request deadline, which no corpus case can wait for. A third shape joined them here: a per-IP cap that QUEUES the connection beyond its limit rather than dropping it. That is what a real cap does, and it deadlocks a client that pools idle connections — the permit is held for the connection's lifetime and an idle pooled connection never releases it — so the only observable is again a five-minute timeout. It was designed, costed and skipped rather than written as a case that could not run.
backlog.rationale: Three named pathologies unreachable for one missing parameter is the argument for implementing it, and the list belongs where the implementation is planned

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10 by running two cases that could not be made to fire. Any pathology whose trigger is 'a connection opens while other connections are transferring' is unreachable in S3, because the fixed pool opens every connection before any body streams. Two shapes died on this. Peer eviction — a new connection cuts one that is mid-response, which is what a hostile anti-leech origin does — never fires at all: the registry of live bodies is empty at every accept. A cap with a memory, where exceeding it locks the source out for a window, is unreachable at socket level for the same reason; extended to block the source it does fire, and then drops the in-flight requests of every worker at once, so the shared retry budget is spent by however many happened to be mid-request when the window opened and two of three runs failed. Both were removed rather than tuned until green. They become reachable when concurrency is adaptive and the pool adds connections during a transfer, which is S4, and the capabilities are worth rebuilding then.
backlog.rationale: A shape that cannot fire is worse than a missing one because the case looks like coverage; recording the class stops the next session rediscovering it

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10, and the reason the connections floor is 19 rather than 20 by padding. Two cases written this session were vacuous when first green and were caught by mutation, not by review. keep-alive-is-declined-in-advance asserted that an origin announcing Connection: close needs no recovery; removing the header left every assertion green, because the origin still closed the connection and the engine still used one request per socket — there is no observable difference on this stack between an announced close and a silent one, which makes it a second copy of keep-alive-closed-after-one-request. It was deleted. an-extra-unsolicited-response-desyncs-the-connection asserted only that the extra response had been written; measuring the run showed three requests across three connections, so no request ever met the poisoned socket and the corruption path was never approached. It was repaired with max_requests_per_connection: 1, which is red when the duplicate is removed because a healthy origin carries the probe and the first range on one connection. The lesson for the remaining categories: an assertion that the pathology was ENACTED is not an assertion that it was ENCOUNTERED.
backlog.rationale: Two of thirteen new proofs could not fail on first writing, which is the rate to expect and the argument for mutating every one

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10. When an origin withdraws range support after the probe proved it — a 206 for the probe and 200 with the whole representation for every ranged request after — the engine fails the transfer. docs/01 section 3.1 says the answer to a 200 for a range request is to treat it as no range support, which taken to its conclusion means re-probing and finishing on a single stream, exactly as the engine already does when ranges are absent at probe time. Nothing is corrupted and nothing is renamed, so this is a robustness gap and not a Category 1 one, and tests/corpus/cases/connections/range-support-is-withdrawn-after-the-probe-proved-it asserts the current error kind with a comment saying it is asserted as it is rather than as it should be. Doing better means a mid-transfer re-probe with its own proofs, and the fallback it would reach is S3-C4's, which is written against absence at probe time.
backlog.rationale: A download that could have finished on one stream instead fails, and the case that would have to change is already marked so it cannot be fixed silently

backlog.text: FOUND 2026-08-10 while hunting the twentieth connections shape. The corpus cannot enact a TCP reset that follows a COMPLETE response, and therefore cannot reach one branch of the engine. SO_LINGER(0) is the only way to make tokio send RST, and it discards the send buffer as well: with a 256 KiB body the client received 196 608 of 262 144 bytes and reported an ordinary truncated_body, which is the case transient-reset-is-retried already covers. So an RST is indistinguishable from a graceful truncation here, and crates/downpour-http/src/h1h2.rs's branch that classifies a body-read error arriving after every promised byte as Transport rather than TruncatedBody has no test and cannot get one from this harness. Worth knowing: with a declared length hyper stops at that length and returns Ok(None) without another read, so the branch may be reachable only with close-delimited framing, where treating the abort as a failure is correct anyway. A fix that let a completed message survive the abort was written and reverted for want of a test that could reach it. Also worth recording: both cases named for resets enact a graceful FIN after a short body, so the category's name for this event has always been aspirational.
backlog.rationale: An unreachable branch in the transfer path is untested by construction, and the name of the two cases that look like they cover it hides that
